lesson_scope: Equilibrium of three coplanar forces acting at a point; resolving forces along chosen orthogonal axes to determine an unknown magnitude and direction; application of closed triangles of forces and Lami's theorem; equilibrium on smooth inclines and with smooth rings; and perpendicular resolution techniques to isolate unknown forces.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 1: Third force balancing two perpendicular forces in equilibrium

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 1: Third force balancing two perpendicular forces in equilibrium

hints: In equilibrium, the sum of all forces is zero, so the third force must equal the negative of the resultant of the first two forces: $\mathbf{F} = -(12\mathbf{i} + 16\mathbf{j})$.
Calculate the magnitude using Pythagoras theorem $|\mathbf{F}| = \sqrt{(-12)^2 + (-16)^2}$, and find the direction using $\tan\theta = \frac{16}{12}$.

walkthrough.text:
Set the sum of forces along each axis to zero in equilibrium:
$$\Sigma F_x = 12 + F_x = 0 \implies F_x = -12\text{ N}$$
$$\Sigma F_y = 16 + F_y = 0 \implies F_y = -16\text{ N}$$

Calculate the magnitude and direction of $\mathbf{F}$:
$$|\mathbf{F}| = \sqrt{(-12)^2 + (-16)^2} = \sqrt{144 + 256} = \sqrt{400} = 20\text{ N}$$
$$\tan\theta = \frac{|F_y|}{|F_x|} = \frac{16}{12} = \frac{4}{3} \implies \theta = \arctan\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \approx 53.13^\circ \approx 53.1^\circ$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Equilibrium means all external pulls cancel out completely to zero:
- The $12\text{ N}$ force pulls directly rightwards along $+x$.
- The $16\text{ N}$ force pulls directly upwards along $+y$.
To cancel both pulls simultaneously, the third force $\mathbf{F}$ must point into the third quadrant:
$$F_x = -12\text{ N}, \quad F_y = -16\text{ N}$$

Combine these rectangular components to find the total pull and direction:
- Magnitude of force $\mathbf{F}$:
$$|\mathbf{F}| = \sqrt{12^2 + 16^2} = \sqrt{400} = 20\text{ N}$$
- Direction angle below the negative $x$-axis:
$$\tan\theta = \frac{16}{12} \implies \theta = \arctan(1.3333) \approx 53.1^\circ$$

ai_rubric.observable: Applies equilibrium condition $\Sigma F_x = 0$ and $\Sigma F_y = 0$ to get components $F_x = -12\text{ N}$ and $F_y = -16\text{ N}$.
Obtains magnitude $|\mathbf{F}| = 20\text{ N}$ and angle $\theta = \arctan(16/12) \approx 53.1^\circ$ (or $0.927\text{ rad}$).

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 2: Finding unknown force magnitude and angle from two known forces

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 2: Finding unknown force magnitude and angle from two known forces

hints: Resolve horizontally to balance the forces: $P\cos\theta = 30 + 40\cos 60^\circ$.
Resolve vertically to balance the forces: $P\sin\theta = 40\sin 60^\circ$, then apply Pythagoras $P = \sqrt{(P\cos\theta)^2 + (P\sin\theta)^2}$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve forces horizontally and vertically in equilibrium:
$$\Sigma F_x = 30 + 40\cos 60^\circ - P\cos\theta = 0 \implies P\cos\theta = 30 + 40(0.5) = 50\text{ N}$$
$$\Sigma F_y = 40\sin 60^\circ - P\sin\theta = 0 \implies P\sin\theta = 40\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.641\text{ N}$$

Calculate the magnitude $P$ using Pythagoras theorem:
$$P = \sqrt{50^2 + (20\sqrt{3})^2} = \sqrt{2500 + 1200} = \sqrt{3700} = 10\sqrt{37} \approx 60.8276 \approx 60.8\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Balance the forces along each coordinate axis:
- Horizontal axis: The $30\text{ N}$ force and the horizontal component of the $40\text{ N}$ force pull rightwards. Force $P$ must balance them by pulling leftwards:
$$P\cos\theta = 30 + 40\cos 60^\circ = 30 + 20 = 50\text{ N}$$
- Vertical axis: The $40\text{ N}$ force pulls upwards with $40\sin 60^\circ = 20\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$. Force $P$ must balance this by pulling downwards:
$$P\sin\theta = 20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.641\text{ N}$$

Combine both components to find the total magnitude $P$:
- Use the Pythagorean identity $(P\cos\theta)^2 + (P\sin\theta)^2 = P^2$:
$$P = \sqrt{50^2 + (20\sqrt{3})^2} = \sqrt{2500 + 1200} = \sqrt{3700} = 10\sqrt{37} \approx 60.8\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves horizontally and vertically in equilibrium: $P\cos\theta = 30 + 40\cos 60^\circ = 50$ and $P\sin\theta = 40\sin 60^\circ = 20\sqrt{3}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 3: Particle suspended by string and horizontal force

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 3: Particle suspended by string and horizontal force

hints: Identify the three forces: downward weight $W = mg = 3(10) = 30\text{ N}$, horizontal pull $15\text{ N}$, and tension $T$ at angle $\theta$ to the vertical.
Form the component equations: $T\sin\theta = 15$ and $T\cos\theta = 30$. Divide them to find $\tan\theta = 0.5$, and use Pythagoras to find $T$.

walkthrough.text:
Set up the horizontal and vertical equilibrium equations:
$$\Sigma F_x = T\sin\theta - 15 = 0 \implies T\sin\theta = 15\text{ N}$$
$$\Sigma F_y = T\cos\theta - mg = 0 \implies T\cos\theta = 3(10) = 30\text{ N}$$

Divide the equations to find $\theta$ and use Pythagoras to find $T$:
$$\tan\theta = \frac{T\sin\theta}{T\cos\theta} = \frac{15}{30} = 0.5 \implies \theta = \arctan(0.5) \approx 26.565^\circ \approx 26.6^\circ$$
$$T = \sqrt{15^2 + 30^2} = \sqrt{225 + 900} = \sqrt{1125} = 15\sqrt{5} \approx 33.541 \approx 33.5\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Notice the geometry of the string angle with the vertical:
- Weight acts vertically downwards: $W = mg = 3 \times 10 = 30\text{ N}$.
- The upward component of tension supports this weight: $T\cos\theta = 30\text{ N}$.
- The horizontal pull is $15\text{ N}$, balanced by the horizontal tension component: $T\sin\theta = 15\text{ N}$.
$$W = 30\text{ N}, \quad T\cos\theta = 30\text{ N}, \quad T\sin\theta = 15\text{ N}$$

Solve for angle $\theta$ and tension $T$:
- Divide horizontal by vertical to eliminate $T$:
$$\tan\theta = \frac{15}{30} = 0.5 \implies \theta = \arctan(0.5) \approx 26.6^\circ$$
- Apply Pythagoras theorem to find the hypotenuse tension $T$:
$$T = \sqrt{15^2 + 30^2} = \sqrt{1125} = 15\sqrt{5} \approx 33.5\text{ N}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 4: Closed right-angled triangle of forces

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 4: Closed right-angled triangle of forces

hints: When three coplanar forces are in equilibrium, their vectors form a closed triangle.
Check the squares of the sides: $8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289$ and $17^2 = 289$. The triangle is right-angled at the vertex between the $8\text{ N}$ and $15\text{ N}$ forces.

walkthrough.text:
Test the side lengths of the closed triangle of forces using Pythagoras theorem:
$$8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289$$
$$17^2 = 289$$
Since $8^2 + 15^2 = 17^2$, the force triangle is right-angled with the $17\text{ N}$ force acting as the hypotenuse.

Determine the angle between the $8\text{ N}$ force and the $15\text{ N}$ force:
In a right-angled force triangle, the angle between the two shorter sides (legs) is $90^\circ$. Therefore, the lines of action of the $8\text{ N}$ and $15\text{ N}$ forces are perpendicular:
$$\phi = 90^\circ$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Recall the fundamental principle of three-force equilibrium:
- The three force vectors must join head-to-tail to form a closed triangle.
- The side lengths of this triangle are $8\text{ N}$, $15\text{ N}$, and $17\text{ N}$.
Check the Pythagorean condition:
$$8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289 = 17^2$$

Interpret the geometric angle:
- Because the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, the angle between the $8\text{ N}$ side and the $15\text{ N}$ side inside the closed triangle is exactly $90^\circ$.
- Thus, the two forces act at right angles to each other:
$$\text{Angle} = 90^\circ$$

ai_rubric.observable: Applies the converse of Pythagoras theorem $8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289 = 17^2$ or the cosine rule.
Deduces that the angle between the $8\text{ N}$ force and the $15\text{ N}$ force is $90^\circ$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 5: Unknown magnitude and angle in second quadrant equilibrium

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 5: Unknown magnitude and angle in second quadrant equilibrium

hints: Set the horizontal forces in equilibrium: $P\cos\theta = 24\text{ N}$.
Set the vertical forces in equilibrium: $P\sin\theta = 18\text{ N}$. Divide to find $\tan\theta = \frac{18}{24} = 0.75$, then use Pythagoras to find $P$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve along the coordinate axes in equilibrium:
$$\Sigma F_x = 24 - P\cos\theta = 0 \implies P\cos\theta = 24\text{ N}$$
$$\Sigma F_y = P\sin\theta - 18 = 0 \implies P\sin\theta = 18\text{ N}$$

Determine the angle $\theta$ and the magnitude $P$:
$$\tan\theta = \frac{P\sin\theta}{P\cos\theta} = \frac{18}{24} = 0.75 \implies \theta = \arctan(0.75) \approx 36.8699^\circ \approx 36.9^\circ$$
$$P = \sqrt{24^2 + 18^2} = \sqrt{576 + 324} = \sqrt{900} = 30\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Identify what force $P$ must balance:
- A horizontal pull of $24\text{ N}$ to the right must be countered by $P\cos\theta = 24\text{ N}$ to the left.
- A vertical downward pull of $18\text{ N}$ must be countered by $P\sin\theta = 18\text{ N}$ upwards:
$$P\cos\theta = 24\text{ N}, \quad P\sin\theta = 18\text{ N}$$

Calculate the magnitude $P$ and angle $\theta$:
- Magnitude from Pythagoras theorem:
$$P = \sqrt{24^2 + 18^2} = \sqrt{900} = 30\text{ N}$$
- Direction angle above the negative $x$-axis:
$$\tan\theta = \frac{18}{24} = 0.75 \implies \theta = \arctan(0.75) \approx 36.9^\circ$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 6: Application of Lami's theorem in three-force equilibrium

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 6: Application of Lami's theorem in three-force equilibrium

hints: The angles around a point sum to $360^\circ$, so the third angle is $360^\circ - 120^\circ - 90^\circ = 150^\circ$.
Apply Lami's theorem: each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two forces: $\frac{T}{\sin 150^\circ} = \frac{10}{\sin 90^\circ}$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the third angle between the $10\text{ N}$ force and force $W$:
$$\text{Angle} = 360^\circ - 120^\circ - 90^\circ = 150^\circ$$

Apply Lami's theorem to find $T$:
$$\frac{T}{\sin 150^\circ} = \frac{10}{\sin 90^\circ}$$
Since $\sin 90^\circ = 1$ and $\sin 150^\circ = \sin(180^\circ - 30^\circ) = \frac{1}{2}$:
$$T = 10\sin 150^\circ = 10(0.5) = 5\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Find the complete set of angles around the equilibrium point:
- Angle between $10\text{ N}$ and $T$: $120^\circ$.
- Angle between $T$ and $W$: $90^\circ$.
- Remaining angle between $10\text{ N}$ and $W$:
$$\text{Angle} = 360^\circ - (120^\circ + 90^\circ) = 360^\circ - 210^\circ = 150^\circ$$

Use Lami's theorem to relate the forces directly to their opposite angles:
- The angle opposite force $T$ is the angle between the other two forces ($150^\circ$).
- The angle opposite the $10\text{ N}$ force is the angle between $T$ and $W$ ($90^\circ$).
Equate their sine ratios:
$$\frac{T}{\sin 150^\circ} = \frac{10}{\sin 90^\circ}$$
$$T = 10 \times \frac{1}{2} = 5\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates the third angle $360^\circ - 120^\circ - 90^\circ = 150^\circ$ and sets up Lami's theorem: $\frac{T}{\sin 150^\circ} = \frac{10}{\sin 90^\circ}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 1: Suspended particle held by horizontal force with Pythagorean ratio

hints: The upward vertical component of tension must support the entire weight of $48\text{ N}$: $T\cos\alpha = 48$.
Substitute $\cos\alpha = \frac{12}{13}$ to solve for $T$: $T\left(\frac{12}{13}\right) = 48 \implies T = 48 \times \frac{13}{12} = 52\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Set up the vertical equilibrium equation:
$$\Sigma F_y = T\cos\alpha - 48 = 0 \implies T\cos\alpha = 48$$

Substitute the exact cosine value and solve for $T$:
$$T\left(\frac{12}{13}\right) = 48 \implies T = 48 \times \frac{13}{12} = 4 \times 13 = 52\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Identify the vertical forces acting on the particle in equilibrium:
- The downward gravitational pull (weight) is $48\text{ N}$.
- The upward support is provided entirely by the vertical component of string tension, $T\cos\alpha$.
Set these two equal:
$$T\cos\alpha = 48\text{ N}$$

Substitute the given fraction $\cos\alpha = \frac{12}{13}$:
$$T\left(\frac{12}{13}\right) = 48$$
Multiply both sides by 13 and divide by 12:
$$T = \frac{48 \times 13}{12} = 4 \times 13 = 52\text{ N}$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 1: Suspended particle held by horizontal force with Pythagorean ratio

hints: Resolve horizontally: the applied force $F$ balances the horizontal component of string tension $T\sin\alpha$.
Substitute $T = 52\text{ N}$ and $\sin\alpha = \frac{5}{13}$ to find $F = 52(5/13) = 20\text{ N}$, and calculate $\alpha = \arcsin(5/13)$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve forces horizontally in equilibrium:
$$\Sigma F_x = F - T\sin\alpha = 0 \implies F = T\sin\alpha$$

Substitute $T = 52\text{ N}$ and $\sin\alpha = \frac{5}{13}$ to find $F$:
$$F = 52\left(\frac{5}{13}\right) = 4 \times 5 = 20\text{ N}$$

Calculate the angle $\alpha$:
$$\alpha = \arcsin\left(\frac{5}{13}\right) \approx 22.6199^\circ \approx 22.6^\circ$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Examine the horizontal direction:
- The force $F$ pulls horizontally to the right.
- The horizontal component of the tension pulls to the left with magnitude $T\sin\alpha$.
Set them equal in equilibrium:
$$F = T\sin\alpha$$

Substitute the tension found in part (a):
$$F = 52\left(\frac{5}{13}\right) = 4 \times 5 = 20\text{ N}$$
Notice that the forces $20\text{ N}$, $48\text{ N}$, and $52\text{ N}$ form a classic $5-12-13$ proportional force triangle scaled by 4:
$$20^2 + 48^2 = 400 + 2304 = 2704 = 52^2$$

Determine the angle $\alpha$ with the vertical:

Along the vertical axis:

Resolve vertically: the downward pull $P\sin\theta$ must balance the combined upward pull of both the $35\text{ N}$ vertical force and the vertical component $50\sin 40^\circ$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve horizontally in equilibrium (taking rightwards as positive):
$$\Sigma F_x = 50\cos 40^\circ - P\cos\theta = 0$$
$$P\cos\theta = 50\cos 40^\circ \approx 38.3022 \approx 38.302\text{ N}$$

Resolve vertically in equilibrium (taking upwards as positive):
$$\Sigma F_y = 50\sin 40^\circ + 35 - P\sin\theta = 0$$
$$P\sin\theta = 50\sin 40^\circ + 35 \approx 32.1394 + 35 = 67.1394 \approx 67.139\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Analyze the horizontal equilibrium of the particle:
- Force $\mathbf{F}_1$ pulls rightwards: $+50\cos 40^\circ$.
- Force $\mathbf{F}_2$ is purely vertical, contributing zero horizontally.
- Force $\mathbf{F}_3$ pulls leftwards with component $-P\cos\theta$.
Equate the opposing horizontal effects:
$$P\cos\theta = 50\cos 40^\circ \approx 38.302\text{ N}$$

Analyze the vertical equilibrium of the particle:
- Force $\mathbf{F}_1$ pulls upwards: $+50\sin 40^\circ \approx 32.139\text{ N}$.
- Force $\mathbf{F}_2$ pulls upwards: $+35\text{ N}$.
- Force $\mathbf{F}_3$ pulls downwards with component $-P\sin\theta$.
Equate the downward pull to the sum of upward pulls:
$$P\sin\theta = 50\sin 40^\circ + 35 \approx 67.139\text{ N}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Structured Practice: Core Practice 4: Smooth ring threaded on string with horizontal pull

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 4: Smooth ring threaded on string with horizontal pull

hints: A smooth ring has no friction, which means the tension in the string is identical on both sides of the ring.
Set up the vertical equilibrium equation: both string segments pull upwards with vertical components $T\cos 30^\circ$ and $T\cos 60^\circ$, balancing the weight $mg = 0.8(10) = 8\text{ N}$.
Factor out $T$: $T(\cos 30^\circ + \cos 60^\circ) = 8$, substitute $\cos 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}$, then rationalize the denominator.

walkthrough.text:
State the uniform tension property:
Because the ring is smooth, there is no friction between the string and the ring. Hence, the tension $T$ is constant and uniform throughout the entire length of the string:
$$T_{AR} = T_{BR} = T$$

Resolve forces vertically in equilibrium:
$$\Sigma F_y = T\cos 30^\circ + T\cos 60^\circ - mg = 0$$
$$T\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\right) = 0.8(10) = 8\text{ N}$$
$$T\left(\frac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{2}\right) = 8 \implies T = \frac{16}{\sqrt{3} + 1}$$

Rationalize the denominator to obtain the exact surd value:
$$T = \frac{16(\sqrt{3} - 1)}{(\sqrt{3} + 1)(\sqrt{3} - 1)} = \frac{16(\sqrt{3} - 1)}{3 - 1} = 8(\sqrt{3} - 1)\text{ N} \approx 5.8564 \approx 5.86\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Explain the physical principle of a smooth bead or ring:
- A knot would divide the string into two separate tensions.
- But a smooth ring allows the string to slide freely without resistance, guaranteeing equal tension $T$ on both sides:
$$T_{AR} = T_{BR} = T$$

Set up vertical force balance:
- Downward weight: $W = mg = 0.8 \times 10 = 8\text{ N}$.
- Upward pull from segment $AR$: $T\cos 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}T$.
- Upward pull from segment $BR$: $T\cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}T$.
Combine the upward components:
$$T\left(\frac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{2}\right) = 8\text{ N}$$

Solve for tension $T$ by multiplying by the conjugate $(\sqrt{3}-1)$:
$$T = \frac{16}{\sqrt{3} + 1} = \frac{16(\sqrt{3} - 1)}{2} = 8(\sqrt{3} - 1)\text{ N} \approx 5.86\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.observable: States that the ring is smooth, so friction is zero and tension $T$ is uniform across both segments $AR$ and $BR$.
Resolves vertically in equilibrium: $T\cos 30^\circ + T\cos 60^\circ = 0.8g = 8\text{ N}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 4: Smooth ring threaded on string with horizontal pull

hints: Resolve horizontally: the ring is pulled to the left by $X$ and segment $AR$ ($T\sin 30^\circ$), and to the right by segment $BR$ ($T\sin 60^\circ$).
Form the horizontal balance equation: $X = T(\sin 60^\circ - \sin 30^\circ)$.
Substitute $T = 8(\sqrt{3}-1)$ and $\sin 60^\circ - \sin 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2}$, then expand the product.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve forces horizontally in equilibrium:
$$\Sigma F_x = T\sin 60^\circ - T\sin 30^\circ - X = 0 \implies X = T(\sin 60^\circ - \sin 30^\circ)$$

Substitute the exact values of the sines:
$$\sin 60^\circ - \sin 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{2}$$

Multiply by the tension $T = 8(\sqrt{3} - 1)$ to find $X$:
$$X = 8(\sqrt{3} - 1)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{2}\right) = 4(\sqrt{3} - 1)^2 = 4(3 - 2\sqrt{3} + 1) = 4(4 - 2\sqrt{3}) = 16 - 8\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$$
$$X \approx 16 - 8(1.73205) = 16 - 13.8564 = 2.1436 \approx 2.14\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Set up horizontal force balance:
- String segment $BR$ pulls to the right: $+T\sin 60^\circ$.
- String segment $AR$ pulls to the left: $-T\sin 30^\circ$.
- The applied force $X$ pulls to the left: $-X$.
Equating leftward pulls to rightward pulls gives:
$$X = T(\sin 60^\circ - \sin 30^\circ)$$

Substitute the exact trigonometric difference:
$$\sin 60^\circ - \sin 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{2}$$
Now multiply by $T = 8(\sqrt{3} - 1)$:
$$X = 8(\sqrt{3} - 1) \times \frac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{2} = 4(\sqrt{3} - 1)^2$$

Expand the squared binomial:
$$(\sqrt{3} - 1)^2 = 3 - 2\sqrt{3} + 1 = 4 - 2\sqrt{3}$$
$$X = 4(4 - 2\sqrt{3}) = 16 - 8\sqrt{3}\text{ N} \approx 2.14\text{ N}$$

The component of the particle's weight down the plane is $mg\sin 30^\circ$.
Set the upward component of the applied force $P\cos\theta$ equal to $mg\sin 30^\circ$, with $mg = 2.5(10) = 25\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the weight of the particle:
$$W = mg = 2.5(10) = 25\text{ N}$$

Resolve forces parallel to the plane in equilibrium:
$$\Sigma F_{\parallel} = P\cos\theta - mg\sin 30^\circ = 0$$
$$P\cos\theta = 25\sin 30^\circ = 25(0.5) = 12.5\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Set up axes aligned with the slope:
- Parallel to the slope (upwards is positive).
- Perpendicular to the slope (normal reaction direction).
Calculate the total gravitational weight:
$$W = mg = 2.5(10) = 25\text{ N}$$

Balance forces along the slope:
- Downward slope pull from gravity: $W\sin 30^\circ = 25 \times 0.5 = 12.5\text{ N}$.
- Upward slope pull from force $P$: $P\cos\theta$.
Equating them for equilibrium:
$$P\cos\theta = 12.5\text{ N}$$

Isolate the trigonometric ratio:

Evaluate the angle:

hints: Resolve perpendicular to the incline: the normal reaction $R_N$ and the perpendicular component of the applied force $P\sin\theta$ both point away from the plane.
Set their sum equal to the perpendicular component of weight: $R_N + P\sin\theta = mg\cos 30^\circ$.
Compute $mg\cos 30^\circ = 25\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \approx 21.651\text{ N}$ and $P\sin\theta = 15\sin(33.56^\circ) \approx 8.292\text{ N}$, then subtract.

walkthrough.text:
Set up the perpendicular equilibrium equation:
$$\Sigma F_{\perp} = R_N + P\sin\theta - mg\cos 30^\circ = 0$$
$$R_N = mg\cos 30^\circ - P\sin\theta$$

Evaluate the trigonometric quantities using $\cos\theta = \frac{5}{6}$:
$$\sin\theta = \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{25}{36}} = \frac{\sqrt{11}}{6} \approx 0.55277$$
$$P\sin\theta = 15\left(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}\right) = 2.5\sqrt{11} \approx 8.2916\text{ N}$$

Calculate the normal reaction $R_N$:
$$R_N = 25\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) - 2.5\sqrt{11} = 12.5\sqrt{3} - 2.5\sqrt{11}$$
$$R_N \approx 21.6506 - 8.2916 = 13.359 \approx 13.4\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Analyze the forces pressing into or lifting off the incline:
- The component of weight pushing into the plane is $mg\cos 30^\circ = 25 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 21.651\text{ N}$.
- Because the force $P$ pulls at an angle $\theta$ above the slope, its upward component $P\sin\theta$ helps lift the particle slightly off the surface.
- The normal reaction $R_N$ provides the remaining support:
$$R_N + P\sin\theta = mg\cos 30^\circ$$

Calculate the lifting effect of force $P$:
- Using $\sin\theta = \sqrt{1 - (5/6)^2} = \frac{\sqrt{11}}{6} \approx 0.5528$:
$$P\sin\theta = 15 \times 0.5528 \approx 8.292\text{ N}$$

Subtract to find the normal reaction:
$$R_N = 21.651 - 8.292 = 13.359 \approx 13.4\text{ N}$$
The normal force exerted by the plane is reduced to $13.4\text{ N}$ because force $P$ partially lifts the particle.

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves perpendicular to the plane: $R_N + P\sin\theta = mg\cos 30^\circ$.

hints: Check the converse of Pythagoras theorem on the side lengths $0.6\text{ m}$, $0.8\text{ m}$, and $1.0\text{ m}$.
Since $0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1.0^2$, the triangle $\triangle APB$ is right-angled at $P$, meaning the two strings are perpendicular.
In right-angled triangle $\triangle APB$, the angle $\angle PAB = \alpha$ has adjacent side $AP = 0.6$ and hypotenuse $AB = 1.0$, so $\cos\alpha = 0.6$.
Similarly, $\cos\beta = \frac{BP}{AB} = \frac{0.8}{1.0} = 0.8$, so $\beta = \arccos(0.8) \approx 36.9^\circ$.

walkthrough.text:
Verify that $\triangle APB$ is a right-angled triangle using the converse of Pythagoras theorem:
$$AP^2 + BP^2 = 0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1.00 = 1.0^2 = AB^2$$
Because $AP^2 + BP^2 = AB^2$, the angle at $P$ is a right angle:
$$\angle APB = 90^\circ$$

Calculate the angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with the horizontal ceiling:
$$\cos\alpha = \frac{AP}{AB} = \frac{0.6}{1.0} = 0.6 \implies \alpha = \arccos(0.6) \approx 53.1301^\circ \approx 53.1^\circ$$
$$\cos\beta = \frac{BP}{AB} = \frac{0.8}{1.0} = 0.8 \implies \beta = \arccos(0.8) \approx 36.8699^\circ \approx 36.9^\circ$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Inspect the geometry of the suspension frame:
- Length $AP = 0.6\text{ m}$.
- Length $BP = 0.8\text{ m}$.
- Ceiling span $AB = 1.0\text{ m}$.
Check the Pythagorean triple $6-8-10$ scaled by $0.1$:
$$0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1.00 = 1.0^2$$
This confirms that $\triangle APB$ is right-angled at $P$, which means the two string tensions are perpendicular to one another.

Calculate the angles at the ceiling supports:
- At support $A$: $\cos\alpha = \frac{\text{Adjacent}}{\text{Hypotenuse}} = \frac{0.6}{1.0} = 0.6$.
$$\alpha = \arccos(0.6) \approx 53.1^\circ$$
- At support $B$: $\cos\beta = \frac{\text{Adjacent}}{\text{Hypotenuse}} = \frac{0.8}{1.0} = 0.8$.
$$\beta = \arccos(0.8) \approx 36.9^\circ$$
Notice that $\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$, as expected in a right-angled triangle.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Capstone Practice 1: Two-string suspension forming perpendicular force system

hints: Because strings $AP$ and $BP$ are perpendicular, resolving along the direction of string $AP$ completely eliminates tension $T_B$!

The angle between string $AP$ and the downward vertical is $90^\circ - \alpha = 90^\circ - 53.13^\circ = 36.87^\circ$. The component of weight along $PA$ is $W\cos(36.87^\circ) = W\sin\alpha = 60(0.8)$.
Equate $T_A = 60(0.8) = 48\text{ N}$.
Similarly, resolve along string $BP$: tension $T_A$ has zero component, so $T_B$ balances the component of weight along $PB$: $T_B = W\sin\beta = 60(0.6) = 36\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Identify the angles between the vertical weight $W = 60\text{ N}$ and the two strings:
$$\angle(\mathbf{W}, AP) = 90^\circ - 53.13^\circ = 36.87^\circ, \quad \angle(\mathbf{W}, BP) = 90^\circ - 36.87^\circ = 53.13^\circ$$

Resolve along string $AP$ (perpendicular to string $BP$):
$$\Sigma F_{AP} = T_A - W\cos(36.87^\circ) = 0$$
$$T_A = 60\cos(36.87^\circ) = 60(0.8) = 48\text{ N}$$

Resolve along string $BP$ (perpendicular to string $AP$):
$$\Sigma F_{BP} = T_B - W\cos(53.13^\circ) = 0$$
$$T_B = 60\cos(53.13^\circ) = 60(0.6) = 36\text{ N}$$

Confirm horizontal equilibrium:
$$T_A\cos\alpha - T_B\cos\beta = 48(0.6) - 36(0.8) = 28.8 - 28.8 = 0\text{ N}$$
Both tensions are verified: $T_A = 48\text{ N}$ and $T_B = 36\text{ N}$.

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Choose the most efficient axes for resolution:
- Because the strings are perpendicular, resolving along string $AP$ completely ignores string $BP$:
$$\angle APB = 90^\circ \implies \mathbf{T}_A \cdot \mathbf{T}_B = 0$$
- Likewise, resolving along string $BP$ completely ignores string $AP$.

Find tension $T_A$ by resolving along $AP$:
- The angle between string $AP$ and the downward vertical is $90^\circ - \alpha = 36.87^\circ$.
- The component of weight pulling along string $AP$ is:
$$W\cos(36.87^\circ) = 60 \times 0.8 = 48\text{ N}$$
Equating this to tension $T_A$ gives:
$$T_A = 48\text{ N}$$

Find tension $T_B$ by resolving along $BP$:
- The angle between string $BP$ and the downward vertical is $90^\circ - \beta = 53.13^\circ$.
- The component of weight pulling along string $BP$ is:
$$W\cos(53.13^\circ) = 60 \times 0.6 = 36\text{ N}$$
Equating this to tension $T_B$ gives:
$$T_B = 36\text{ N}$$

Double-check with Pythagoras on the tension triangle:
- The two tensions and the weight form a closed right-angled triangle:
$$T_A^2 + T_B^2 = 48^2 + 36^2 = 2304 + 1296 = 3600 = 60^2 = W^2$$
This verifies the solution.

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves along string $AP$ or sets up horizontal balance: $T_A\cos\alpha = T_B\cos\beta$.
Resolves along string $BP$ or sets up vertical balance: $T_A\sin\alpha + T_B\sin\beta = 60$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Capstone Practice 2: Optimization of holding force in angled string equilibrium

hints: Notice the direction of the string: it makes $60^\circ$ with the vertical, which is $30^\circ$ with the horizontal.
A direction perpendicular to the string makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the vertical, or $60^\circ$ below the horizontal.
The angle between force $P$ (at $\theta$ above horizontal) and the perpendicular to the string (at $30^\circ$ above horizontal) is $\theta - 30^\circ$.
Resolve perpendicular to the string: tension $T$ has zero component, the weight has component $80\sin 60^\circ$, so $P\cos(\theta - 30^\circ) = 80\sin 60^\circ = 40\sqrt{3}$.

walkthrough.text:
Explain why tension $T$ does not appear in the perpendicular equation:
$$\Sigma F_\perp: \quad T_\perp = T\cos 90^\circ = 0\text{ N}$$

Determine the angles of the forces relative to the perpendicular to the string:
The string is inclined at $60^\circ$ to the downward vertical, so the perpendicular direction makes an angle of $90^\circ - 60^\circ = 30^\circ$ with the horizontal.
The component of the weight $W = 80\text{ N}$ perpendicular to the string is:
$$W_\perp = 80\sin 60^\circ = 80\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 40\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$$
The force $P$ acts at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal, so its angle with the perpendicular to the string is $\theta - 30^\circ$.

Set up the perpendicular equilibrium equation:
$$\Sigma F_\perp = P\cos(\theta - 30^\circ) - 80\sin 60^\circ = 0$$
$$P\cos(\theta - 30^\circ) = 40\sqrt{3}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Understand the power of resolving perpendicular to an unknown force:
- The tension $T$ is directed straight along the string.
- When resolving perpendicular to the string, the tension contributes zero:
$$T\cos 90^\circ = 0$$
This isolates force $P$ directly without having to find $T$ first.

Find the component of the weight perpendicular to the string:
- The string makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the vertical line of gravity.
- The perpendicular component of gravity pulling the particle away from the vertical is:
$$80\sin 60^\circ = 80\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 40\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$$

Find the component of force $P$ along this same perpendicular direction:
- The perpendicular to the string is inclined at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal.
- Force $P$ is inclined at $\theta$ above the horizontal.
- The angle between them is $\theta - 30^\circ$, giving the component $P\cos(\theta - 30^\circ)$.
Equating the two gives:
$$P\cos(\theta - 30^\circ) = 40\sqrt{3}$$

ai_rubric.observable: States that tension $T$ acts along the string, so its component perpendicular to the string is $T\cos 90^\circ = 0$.
Resolves perpendicular to the string: component of weight is $80\sin 60^\circ$, and component of $P$ is $P\cos(\theta - 30^\circ)$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Capstone Practice 2: Optimization of holding force in angled string equilibrium

hints: From $P = \frac{40\sqrt{3}}{\cos(\theta - 30^\circ)}$, $P$ is minimized when the denominator is maximized.
The maximum value of $\cos(\theta - 30^\circ)$ is $1$, which occurs when $\theta - 30^\circ = 0 \implies \theta = 30^\circ$.
This gives $P_{\min} = 40\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$, meaning force $P$ is applied perpendicular to the string.
Resolve along the string: since $P$ is perpendicular to the string, it has zero component along the string, so $T = 80\cos 60^\circ = 40\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Minimize $P$ by maximizing the cosine term:
$$P = \frac{40\sqrt{3}}{\cos(\theta - 30^\circ)}$$
Since $-1 \leqslant \cos(\theta - 30^\circ) \leqslant 1$, the maximum value of the denominator is $1$:
$$\cos(\theta - 30^\circ) = 1 \implies \theta - 30^\circ = 0^\circ \implies \theta = 30^\circ$$
$$P_{\min} = \frac{40\sqrt{3}}{1} = 40\sqrt{3} \approx 69.282 \approx 69.3\text{ N}$$

Resolve along the line of the string to find tension $T$:
When $\theta = 30^\circ$, force $P$ acts exactly perpendicular to the string, so its component along the string is zero:
$$\Sigma F_\parallel = T - W\cos 60^\circ = 0$$
$$T = 80\cos 60^\circ = 80(0.5) = 40\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Understand why perpendicularity minimizes the required holding force:
- Any component of $P$ that acts along the string only fights or assists tension, without helping to pull the particle sideways.
- To produce the required sideways balancing pull with minimal effort, $P$ must be directed purely perpendicular to the string:
$$\theta = 30^\circ$$

State the minimum magnitude:
$$P_{\min} = 40\sqrt{3} \approx 69.3\text{ N}$$

Find the resulting string tension:
- Because force $P$ acts purely perpendicular to the string, it does not support any portion of the weight along the string's length.
- The string tension must support the entire component of weight along the string:
$$T = 80\cos 60^\circ = 80 \times 0.5 = 40\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Uses $\cos(\theta - 30^\circ) \leqslant 1$ to deduce that $P$ is minimized when $\cos(\theta - 30^\circ) = 1$.
Resolves along the string to obtain $T = 80\cos 60^\circ = 40\text{ N}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Capstone Practice 2: Optimization of holding force in angled string equilibrium

hints: When $P$ is horizontal, resolve vertically to find $T$: the upward component of tension $T\cos 60^\circ$ must support the weight of $80\text{ N}$.
Calculate $T = \frac{80}{\cos 60^\circ} = \frac{80}{0.5} = 160\text{ N}$.
Resolve horizontally: the horizontal component of tension $T\sin 60^\circ$ balances $P$, so $P = 160\sin 60^\circ = 160\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 80\sqrt{3} \approx 139\text{ N}$.
State both values: the tension in the string is $T = 160\text{ N}$, and the required horizontal pull is $P = 80\sqrt{3} \approx 139\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve vertically in equilibrium with a horizontal applied force $P$:
$$\Sigma F_y = T\cos 60^\circ - 80 = 0$$
$$T = \frac{80}{\cos 60^\circ} = \frac{80}{0.5} = 160\text{ N}$$

Resolve horizontally in equilibrium:
$$\Sigma F_x = P - T\sin 60^\circ = 0$$
$$P = 160\sin 60^\circ = 160\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 80\sqrt{3} \approx 138.564 \approx 139\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Compare this case with the optimal configuration from part (b):
- Pulling horizontally means force $P$ does not provide any upward lifting assistance.
- The string must support the entire vertical weight by itself:
$$T\cos 60^\circ = 80\text{ N}$$
$$T = \frac{80}{0.5} = 160\text{ N}$$
Notice that the tension has quadrupled from $40\text{ N}$ to $160\text{ N}$!

Find the required horizontal pull $P$:
- The horizontal component of this larger tension must be balanced by $P$:
$$P = T\sin 60^\circ = 160 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 80\sqrt{3} \approx 139\text{ N}$$
Because pulling horizontally is less mechanically efficient, $P$ must be twice as large as the minimum force ($80\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$ compared to $40\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$).

ai_rubric.observable: Sets up equilibrium equations for horizontal force: $T\sin 60^\circ = P$ and $T\cos 60^\circ = 80$.
